content: Participants in the study attended monthly visits where they received HIV testing, personalized risk-reduction counseling, adherence counseling, and were provided with condoms and methadone treatment. Blood safety assessments were conducted every three months. The primary efficacy endpoint of the study was the incidence of HIV infection, analyzed using a modified intention-to-treat approach. The study was registered under the identifier NCT00119106. Between June 9, 2005, and July 22, 2010, a total of 2,413 participants were enrolled in the study. Of these, 1,204 were assigned to receive tenofovir, and 1,209 were assigned to receive a placebo. The findings demonstrated that daily oral tenofovir significantly reduced the risk of HIV infection among people who inject drugs. This suggests that pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) with tenofovir can now be considered as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention strategy for this population. The study was funded by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration. A systematic review of PrEP for people who inject drugs (PWID) was conducted to inform the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations. Surveys were conducted with 1,790 individuals from potential user groups, including female sex workers (FSWs), men who have sex with men (MSM), injecting drug users (IDUs), serodiscordant couples (SDCs), and young women across seven countries: Peru, Ukraine, India, Kenya, Botswana, Uganda, and South Africa. The results showed that 61% of participants expressed a willingness to use PrEP, even when informed about potential side effects, the need for condom use, and regular HIV testing. The route of administration was identified as the most important factor influencing preferences for PrEP. Cost-effectiveness studies of PrEP interventions were reviewed to evaluate their potential impact on health outcomes and resource allocation. Thirteen modeling studies were included, which assessed factors such as prioritization strategies, adherence, behavior change, toxicity, and resistance. The findings indicated that delivering PrEP to populations at the highest risk of HIV exposure is the most cost-effective strategy. However, the results of these analyses must be interpreted within the context of the assumptions made in the models. The Bangkok Tenofovir Study, a phase-3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, was launched in 2005 to evaluate whether daily oral tenofovir could reduce the risk of HIV infection among injecting drug users. A total of 2,413 participants were enrolled, with a median age of 31 years, 80% of whom were male. Among those who injected drugs, 53% reported using methamphetamine, 37% midazolam, and 35% heroin. The study design was adjusted to account for lower-than-expected HIV incidence, increasing the sample size and changing the follow-up period to an endpoint-driven design. Results from the trial were anticipated in 2012. Attitudes toward PrEP among high-risk populations, including drug users, were also investigated. A survey of 190 drug users in western China revealed that 70% had a positive attitude toward PrEP, provided the medication was safe and effective. Factors influencing positive attitudes included awareness of AIDS severity, attitudes toward HIV patients, and knowledge of preventive measures. The study emphasized the importance of education and behavioral interventions to improve attitudes toward PrEP among high-risk populations. Overall, the findings from these studies highlight the potential of PrEP as an effective tool for HIV prevention, particularly among key populations at high risk of exposure. However, successful implementation requires addressing barriers such as cost, adherence, and access, as well as integrating PrEP into broader prevention strategies.
